name: Radcore NeutronVeil Reactor Maintenance Suit
description:
A Class-4 radiation suit manufactured for licensed reactor technicians and illegally resold into Shelf black markets where contaminated zones demand it. The outer shell is a pewter-grey woven lead-polymer fabric — heavy, stiff at the shoulders, with a characteristic forward-lean posture after long wear. Dosimeter patches are stitched at the chest and left forearm; most secondhand suits have patches that are faded or missing entirely.

The suit breaks into five modular sections: torso, two arm assemblies, two leg assemblies — all connected by locking ring seals at joints. A thick polycarbonate helmet dome with integrated air filtration scrubber completes the ensemble. New suits smell of antiseptic; old ones smell of nothing, which is somehow worse.
functionality: Rated for gamma and beta radiation shielding. Modular joint seals allow limited limb replacement if a section is compromised. Integrated air scrubber filters particulate and low-level radioactive dust. Dosimeter patches log cumulative exposure. Aug-routing channels run along the outer forearm seams.
what_it_says: You go where the reactors are cracked and someone has to go in first.
worn_by: black-market rad-suit resellers who test product personally
manufacturer: Radcore Systems (corponation licensed); surplus units through Shelf black market
story_hooks: A secondhand suit on the Shelf market still has the original owner's name stenciled inside the collar — that person is listed as missing in a reactor incident three years ago.
Someone is selling counterfeit Radcore suits with substandard lead-polymer content; the dosimeter patches are cosmetic only.
A reactor tech discovers their suit's scrubber was swapped for a non-functional replica — deliberate sabotage, or a supply chain failure?

physical_description.visual_profile: A bulky, geometric silhouette with pronounced shoulder structure and a forward-lean posture. The figure reads as heavily armored despite being protective rather than combat-oriented. The modular construction creates visible panel lines at shoulders, elbows, hips, and knees. Worn examples show a slightly sagged appearance at the torso from repeated use.
physical_description.fit: Intentionally oversized and rigid. Designed for layering underneath and mobility in contaminated environments rather than body-conforming. The shoulders sit high and squared. Arm and leg assemblies create a slightly robotic gait when worn. Compression is minimal; instead, the suit maintains structural separation from skin.
physical_description.primary_material: Pewter-grey woven lead-polymer composite — heavy, stiff, and chemically treated. The weave is visible as a subtle crosshatch pattern under direct light. Polycarbonate helmet dome with dark tinting and visible internal filtration cartridges.
physical_description.texture: Rough, industrial weave with a matte finish. Joints and seal points show reinforced ribbing. Older suits develop micro-cracks in the polymer shell. Dosimeter patches (faded or missing) create ghost-mark rectangles on chest and forearm. Metal locking rings at joints show wear polish or oxidation depending on condition.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant pewter-grey with matte charcoal accents at seal joints and ring closures. Faded dosimeter patches read as washed-out yellow or tan on secondhand units. Internal filtration cartridges visible through helmet dome in dark grey or black.
physical_description.closures: Locking ring seals at five modular connection points (shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, neck). Friction-fit helmet dome with quarter-turn lock mechanism. No traditional zippers or snaps; the suit is entered by unbolting the torso section or removing the helmet entirely.
distinctive_features: Modular five-piece construction with visible locking ring seals
Polycarbonate helmet dome with integrated air filtration scrubber
Stitched dosimeter patch locations (often faded or missing on secondhand units)
Lead-polymer weave with industrial crosshatch visible pattern
Forward-lean structural bias built into torso and shoulders
Internal cartridge housing visible through transparent helmet sections
Ghost marks from removed or degraded patches
Radcore Systems manufacturer stamp (usually on left shoulder or hip)
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 industrial. New suits Tier 2 (corpo technician). Secondhand black-market units Tier 4-5 (sub-grade contamination workers, scrappers, illegal zone explorers).
physical_description.cultural_context: Signals hazmat work, reactor maintenance, or illegal contamination zone activity. Wearing a Radcore suit without proper licensing marks the wearer as either a licensed technician or someone salvaging/black-marketing protective gear. In the GLMZ, seen frequently among Shelf dwellers, industrial salvagers, and unauthorized zone runners.
physical_description.condition_typical: Secondhand suits show wear at seal points, faded or missing dosimeter patches, micro-cracks in polycarbonate helmet, oxidized locking rings, and a slight chemical smell overtone. New suits are pristine, antiseptic, with bright yellow dosimeter patches and perfectly clear helmets.

Moody cyan-and-amber lighting from above, casting sharp shadows across the suit's rigid shoulder structure and modular panel lines. Close detail on the pewter-grey lead-polymer weave, the locking ring seals at joints, and the polycarbonate helmet dome (slightly fogged, internal filtration cartridges visible). The model's posture shows the characteristic forward-lean of long-term wear. Dosimeter patch ghost-marks visible on chest and forearm.
